procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 13.12.2023 passed by the High Court of Telangana in Criminal Petition No. 12222 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellant moved the High Court of Telangana seeking to quash the Family Court's Order dated 09.06.2023. The High Court modified the Family Court's order, decreasing the interim maintenance payable by the Appellant from INR 20,000 to INR 10,000 per month.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant appealed the High Court's order to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the High Court's order.

directions: The Impugned Order dated 13.12.2023 passed by the High Court of Telangana is affirmed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a petition for maintenance filed by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is maintainable.

facts: The case involves a petition for maintenance filed by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC).

The question arose in light of the subsequent enactment of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which created a specific legal framework for maintenance for divorced Muslim women.
law: Section 125 of the CrPC is a secular provision that allows wives, children, and parents to claim maintenance if they are unable to maintain themselves.
The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, was enacted to specify the rights of divorced Muslim women, including the right to a fair and reasonable provision and maintenance.
The Supreme Court's Constitution Bench decision in *Danial Latifi v. Union of India* upheld the validity of the 1986 Act.
application: The Court relied on its previous Constitution Bench judgment in *Danial Latifi v. Union of India*.
In the *Danial Latifi* case, the Court had interpreted the 1986 Act to mean that a Magistrate has the power to grant maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman.
The Court noted that the parameters and considerations for granting maintenance under the 1986 Act are the same as those under Section 125 of the CrPC.
Therefore, since the Magistrate retains the power to grant maintenance with the same standards, a petition filed under Section 125 CrPC is maintainable.
The Court explicitly stated that a divorced Muslim woman is not restricted from exercising her independent right to maintenance under the secular provision of Section 125 of the CrPC.
It was also clarified that such a petition is maintainable as long as the woman has not remarried, and the maintenance awarded is not restricted to the iddat period only.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a petition for maintenance filed by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is maintainable. Her right under this secular provision is not restricted by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.

issue.issue_text: Whether the acceptance of maintenance by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, bars her from filing a subsequent application under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

facts: The issue concerns a divorced Muslim woman who has accepted maintenance from her ex-husband under Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.

Subsequently, the same woman files an application for maintenance under the secular provision of Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973, on the grounds that she is unable to maintain herself.
The question before the court was whether her initial acceptance of maintenance under the 1986 Act bars her from seeking this subsequent remedy under the CrPC.
law: Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC): A secular provision that allows wives, children, and parents to claim maintenance if they are unable to maintain themselves.

Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986: Provides for a 'reasonable and fair provision and maintenance' to be made and paid to a divorced Muslim woman by her former husband within the iddat period.

Section 127(3)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973: Allows a Magistrate to cancel or vary a maintenance order under Section 125 if the woman has received the whole of the sum which, under any customary or personal law, was payable on such divorce.
application: The Supreme Court determined that a divorced Muslim woman's right to claim maintenance under the secular provision of Section 125 of the CrPC is an independent right.
The Court held that a divorced Muslim woman is not restricted from exercising this right even if she has already received a payment under Section 3 of the 1986 Act.
It was clarified that a divorced Muslim woman is entitled to seek recourse under either or both of the provisions (Section 125 CrPC and the 1986 Act).

To address the concern of 'double payment', the Court pointed out that any amount paid under the 1986 Act would be taken into consideration by the magistrate when deciding on a subsequent application under Section 125 CrPC, as per the mechanism provided in Section 127(3)(b) of the CrPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the acceptance of maintenance by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 3 of the 1986 Act does not bar her from filing a subsequent application for maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC. The remedies under both statutes are available to her, and any prior payment under the 1986 Act will be considered when determining the amount for the subsequent claim.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Family Court has jurisdiction to entertain an application filed by a Muslim divorced woman for maintenance under Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.

facts: The case involved the question of whether a Family Court could hear an application for maintenance filed by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.
law: The Court analyzed the provisions of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, specifically Section 3(2), which states that an application for maintenance should be filed before a competent Magistrate.
The Court also examined the Family Courts Act, 1984, particularly Section 7, which outlines the jurisdiction of Family Courts.
application: The Court found that Section 7 of the Family Courts Act does not grant jurisdiction to Family Courts to entertain applications filed under Section 3 of the 1986 Act.
It determined that the proper forum for such an application is a competent Magistrate, as specified by the 1986 Act itself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Family Court lacks jurisdiction to entertain an application for maintenance from a divorced Muslim woman under Section 3 of the 1986 Act. The Court also held that a Family Court cannot convert a maintenance petition filed under Section 125 of the CrPC into one under the 1986 Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a petition for maintenance filed by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is maintainable.
appellant_arguments: The petition is not maintainable because the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, is a special law that supersedes and overrides the general provisions of Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The non-obstante clauses in Sections 3 and 4 of the 1986 Act establish its prevailing nature over other laws.
The transitional provision in Section 7 of the 1986 Act indicates the legislature's intent for the 1986 Act to be the superseding law.
respondent_arguments: The petition is maintainable as the 1986 Act does not act as a complete bar to claiming maintenance under Section 125 CrPC.
The non-obstante clause in the 1986 Act does not automatically override all other statutory rights available to a divorced Muslim woman.
Previous Supreme Court Constitution Bench rulings have already established that Section 125 CrPC remains applicable.
Section 5 of the 1986 Act, which allows parties to opt to be governed by Section 125 CrPC, confirms that the provision is not automatically overridden.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the acceptance of maintenance by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, bars her from filing a subsequent application under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
appellant_arguments: Yes, it acts as a bar. Since the 1986 Act is a complete and superseding remedy, once a woman accepts maintenance under it, she is precluded from making a subsequent claim under Section 125 CrPC.
respondent_arguments: No, it does not bar a subsequent application. The rights and remedies under Section 125 CrPC are independent and are not extinguished by receiving maintenance under the 1986 Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A non-obstante clause in the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, does not override the right of a divorced Muslim woman to seek maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and both remedies are available.
obiter: The doctrine of stare decisis, as contemplated by Article 141 of the Constitution, binds the court to follow the observations of Constitution Benches.
An interpretative approach to statutes should consider social facts and basic human rights, and enactments should not be construed to intend unjust consequences.
The court's interpretation is consistent with the spirit of Article 15(3) of the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that a petition for maintenance by a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the CrPC is maintainable, as the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, does not override this provision. The court reasoned, based on established precedents and constitutional principles, that the 1986 Act was intended to enhance, not curtail, the rights of divorced Muslim women, making it an additional remedy rather than an exclusive one. Therefore, the non-obstante clause in the 1986 Act does not bar access to the secular, social justice measure provided by Section 125 CrPC.
legal_tests_applied: Doctrine of Stare Decisis (Article 141 of the Constitution): The court explicitly stated it was bound by the conclusions of prior Constitution Benches regarding the interpretation of the 1986 Act and its relationship with Section 125 CrPC.

Interpretation of Non-Obstante Clause: The court applied the principle that a non-obstante clause's impact must be measured in view of the legislative intention and policy, concluding that its purpose was to enhance rights, not to override other beneficial statutes.

Constitutional Interpretation: The court interpreted Section 125 CrPC in light of the principles of social and economic justice enshrined in Articles 15(3) and 39 of the Constitution, which mandate special provisions for women and protection against material abandonment.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's primary argument that the non-obstante clause in the 1986 Act overrides Section 125 CrPC was rejected, as the court, citing precedent, held that such clauses cannot be deemed to automatically override other statutory rights.
The court was bound by the Doctrine of Stare Decisis under Article 141 of the Constitution to follow the established law laid down by previous Constitution Benches on this issue.
The court interpreted Section 7 of the 1986 Act as being 'transitionary in nature' and not indicative of an intent to supersede Section 125 CrPC.

The court found that interpretations of Section 5 of the 1986 Act (which allows parties to opt for Section 125) by numerous previous decisions contradicted the appellant's contention that the 1986 Act was the sole remedy.
The appellant's position was contrary to the established principle from the Khatoon Nisa case, which the court found applicable and determinative on the issue of jurisdiction.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was affirmed because the court reiterated that Section 125 CrPC is a secular measure of social justice applicable to the 'whole community of womanhood,' not confined to any single religion.

The court accepted the interpretation that the legislative intent behind the non-obstante clause in the 1986 Act was to 'enhance the right of a citizen,' not to take away existing rights under Section 125 CrPC.
The respondent's stance was supported by established Supreme Court precedents, including Constitution Bench rulings, which the court was constitutionally bound to follow.

The court aligned the respondent's right to claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC with the constitutional objectives of Articles 15(3) and 39, which mandate state protection for women against distress and abandonment.
policy_considerations: Section 125 of the CrPC is a measure of social justice with a view to protect women and children and is aligned to the salutary object enshrined in Article 15(1) and (3) of the Constitution read with Article 39(e) of the Constitution.

The enactment of Section 125 CrPC charges the court with a deliberate secular design to enforce maintenance or its equivalent against the humane obligation, which is derived from the State’s responsibility for social welfare.
The benefit of doubt, if any, in statutory interpretation belongs to the ill-used wife and the derelict divorcee.

Parliament, in keeping with Article 15(3), deliberately made a special provision to help women in distress cast away by divorce, and protection against moral and material abandonment (Article 39) is part of social and economic justice fundamental to the governance of the country.
